241:
"And for divorced women is a provision according to what is acceptable — a duty upon the righteous."

Beyond specific mahr rules, divorced women are owed mut'ah — a provision in ma'ruf — as a duty on the muttaqin. Taqwa shows in the exit payment and the tone of the exit. The verse generalises care so that no divorced woman is treated as discarded trash because a contract ended. Leaving a marriage is allowed; leaving dignity on the floor is not the sunnah of the righteous.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, remained gentle in separations and commanded kindness. Ma'ruf scales with custom and capacity but never scales to zero from stinginess dressed as "she wanted the divorce" or "her family was difficult." He said the best of you are the best to their wives, and the spirit of that teaching does not evaporate on the day talaq is spoken.

Budget for a dignified provision if you divorce. Speak without smear. The muttaqun leave a gift and a memory that soften a hard page, not a story of humiliation that haunts the children for decades. This short verse is a mirror held up at the door on the way out.

Family rulings are worship when they are lived for Allah's face: patience in anger, fairness in paperwork, mercy in tone. The neighbour and the child are watching how you use power in the house; so is the Lord who wrote these limits.
242:
"Thus does Allah make clear to you His verses that you may use reason."

A seal on the block of family rulings. Clarity is intentional; the goal is that you ta'qilun — reason, understand, internalise. Shariah here is not anti-mind; it trains the mind with cases: iddah, mahr, nursing, prayer in fear. Reason that submits to clear ayat is the reason the Quran praises; reason that hunts fog to escape duty is the "intelligence" it does not honour.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, taught details that fill these frames and said the lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear and between them are doubtful matters. When Allah makes clear, pretending confusion becomes a moral choice, not an intellectual fate. The companions asked when they needed, then acted.

Read family law with the intellect and the heart together. Clarity was given so you would live it, not so you would look for weather to hide in. If a verse in this section still feels locked, seek knowledge with people of adab — then implement what becomes plain. Understanding that never leaves the chair is not the ta'qilun this seal asked for.

243:
"Have you not considered those who left their homes in many thousands, fearing death? Allah said to them, 'Die'; then He restored them to life. And Allah is full of bounty to the people, but most of the people do not show gratitude."

A story-sign: a throng flees death — plague or war in the reports of the commentators — and death meets them by Allah's word anyway; then He raises them, teaching that flight from the decree is not a fortress. Bounty upon people is vast; gratitude is scarce.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, forbade entering a plague land and forbade fleeing it once present, a balanced hadith of means and tawakkul. The point of the ayah is not passivity; it is that ultimate life and death are His, and panic without faith is wasted motion.

Take means. Do not worship means. When He says die, souls leave; when He gives life, excuses die. Be among the grateful few who see bounty in both the taking and the giving back.

244:
"And fight in the cause of Allah and know that Allah is Hearing and Knowing."

After a story about fearing death, the command returns: fight in Allah's path — with the ethics already built in this surah — and know He hears and knows. He hears the intention under the armour, the du'a in the trench, the boast, the secret fear. He knows who fights so that His word be highest and who fights for a banner of pride or plunder.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, said whoever fights so that the word of Allah be highest is in the way of Allah. Hearing and Knowing make show-jihad and secret cowardice equally transparent. He also said the mujahid is the one who strives against his own self in obedience to Allah — widening struggle beyond a single field.

If you struggle in any hard path of His — battlefield, refusing riba, telling truth, holding a family together on halal — clean the niyyah. The audience of record is already Hearing and Knowing. Applause is optional; their witness is not.

Leave the labels that make riba sound clever — 'growth product,' 'convenience fee,' 'time value' dressed to hide excess. The Quran already knew the arguments and still drew the line. Your task is exit with tawbah and principal, not a better brand name for the same war.
245:
"Who is it that would loan Allah a goodly loan so He may multiply it for him many times over? And it is Allah who withholds and grants abundance, and to Him you will be returned."

Charity is framed as a loan to Allah — qard hasan — the most trustworthy borrower. He multiplies it many times, as the grain image of 2:261 will soon picture. Withholding and expanding wealth are His; return is to Him. So the tight fist is not "saving from the universe"; it is refusing a deal with the Owner of the universe.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, said charity does not decrease wealth, and he said Allah says, "Spend, O son of Adam, and I shall spend on you." He also taught that the servant says "my wealth, my wealth," while only three things are truly his: what he ate and wore out, and what he gave and stored for the akhirah. Everything else is left for heirs.

Make the loan. Name it hasan with pure intention and lawful money. Multiplier and return destination are already written in the verse. The only open question is whether you will be among those who answer "who is it that would loan" with their hand, not only with their admiration.

Move something today — even small — while the intention is clean. The verses of spending in this surah are not museum pieces; they are invoices the heart keeps delaying. Pay one before sleep.
246:
"Have you not considered the assembly of the Children of Israel after Musa when they said to a prophet of theirs, 'Send to us a king, and we will fight in the way of Allah'? He said, 'Would you perhaps refrain from fighting if fighting was prescribed for you?' They said, 'And why should we not fight in the way of Allah when we have been driven out from our homes and our children?' But when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away, except a few of them. And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers."

Zeal in theory, collapse in prescription. They demand a king to lead jihad, invoke expulsion of homes and children, then mostly quit when fighting is actually written. A few remain. Allah knows the zalimun who speech-fight then flee the field.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, valued loyalty under pressure over eloquence in safety. He said people are like camels — a hundred and you barely find one fit for riding — a hard metaphor about scarcity of reliability.

Measure yourself by what you do when the cost arrives, not by how moved you feel in a talk about courage. The few who did not turn away are the point of the story; be harder to count among the many who did.

Ethics in conflict are part of faith, not decoration after victory. The same Book that allows force fences it. If your anger cannot accept a fence, it is not yet fighting in the way of Allah.
247:
"And their prophet said to them, 'Indeed, Allah has sent to you Talut as a king.' They said, 'How can he have kingship over us while we are more worthy of kingship than him and he has not been given any measure of wealth?' He said, 'Indeed, Allah has chosen him over you and has increased him abundantly in knowledge and stature. And Allah gives His sovereignty to whom He wills. And Allah is all-Encompassing and Knowing.'"

They wanted a king; they got Talut (Saul) — and immediately snobbery spoke: we are more deserving, he lacks wealth. The prophet answers with Allah's criteria: He chose him, increased him in knowledge and body (capacity), and mulk belongs to Allah to assign. Wasi' and 'Alim — wide in grace, knowing in placement.

The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, appointed leaders for din and competence, including Zayd and Usama over older elites, and he said listen and obey even if a slave is appointed over you. Wealth is not the Quran's primary qualification for rule; knowledge, capacity, and divine placement are.

When leadership goes to someone without your preferred résumé, check for the Children of Israel's disease. Ask whether Allah's measures — knowledge, fitness, trust — are present, not whether your clan's wallet was consulted.

248:
"And their prophet said to them, 'Indeed, a sign of his kingship is that the chest will come to you in which is assurance from your Lord and a remnant of what the family of Musa and the family of Harun had left, carried by the angels. Indeed in that is a sign for you, if you are believers.'"

The return of the Tabut — the ark — with sakinah, reassurance, and relics of Musa and Harun's family, borne by angels, is named as the sign of Talut's legitimate mulk. Believers recognise signs; chronic complainers explain them away even when angels are the porters.

Sakinah is a word the Quran loves: calm poured on hearts at Badr and Hunayn and in the cave (9:26, 9:40, 48:4). The Prophet, peace be upon him, said sakinah descends with Quran recitation. The Israelite ark is particular history; the need for reassurance from Allah is universal. Leadership without sakinah becomes noise; leadership with it steadies nations.

If you are a believer, signs increase you. If you are a debater by addiction, even angels carrying a chest will not end your objections. Choose which audience you are before the next sign arrives — in history, in your own answered du'a, in a door Allah opens after you accepted a leader by His measures rather than by your class prejudice.

249:
"And when Talut went forth with the soldiers, he said, 'Indeed, Allah will be testing you with a river. So whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is indeed of me, excepting one who takes a handful with his hand.' But they drank from it, except a few of them. Then when he had crossed it along with those who believed with him, they said, 'There is no power for us today against Jalut and his soldiers.' But those who were certain that they would meet Allah said, 'How many a small company has overcome a large company by permission of Allah. And Allah is with the patient.'"

A test inside the test: a river on a hot march. Drink freely and you are not with the king; a handful is excused. Most fail — as most failed the earlier zeal. Across the river, numbers look worse against Goliath's army, and panic speaks. Then the people of yaqin who know they will meet Allah answer with a principle: small companies beat large ones by Allah's permission. Allah is with the patient.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, and 313 at Badr lived the principle. He forbade disobedience in the army and prized the few who keep covenants of discipline. Sabr and yaqin, not hydration-plus-panic, decide the story.

Handfuls, not bellies. Certainty of meeting Allah, not headcounts. When your river comes — a pleasure that filters the ranks — drink like a believer on a mission, not like a crowd on a picnic.

250:
"And when they went forth to face Jalut and his soldiers, they said, 'Our Lord, pour upon us patience and plant firmly our feet and give us victory over the disbelieving people.'"

The du'a before impact is a curriculum: pour sabr over us — not a drop, a pouring; fix our feet — no flight; help us against the disbelieving people. Patience, steadfastness, victory — in that moral order. Feet do not plant without sabr; victory is asked after the inner request, not instead of it.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, made du'a at Badr until his cloak fell, saying, "O Allah, if this band perishes, You will not be worshipped on earth." He taught asking for firmness of heart (3:8) and loved concise comprehensive du'a. He also said the du'a of the oppressed is answered — and here the smaller company is the oppressed facing Jalut's machine.

Before your hard face-off — exam, operation, confrontation with injustice, temptation that feels taller than you — borrow this sequence. Pour. Plant. Help. The order keeps you from asking for triumph while planning to run. Then step forward like people who already handed the outcome to the One they asked.

Let the empty stomach teach an empty tongue of false speech and an empty hand of harm. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said whoever does not leave false speech and acting on it, Allah has no need that he leave his food and drink. Fast in full.
251:
"So they defeated them by permission of Allah, and Dawud killed Jalut, and Allah gave him the kingship and wisdom and taught him from that which He willed. And if it were not for Allah checking some people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted, but Allah is full of bounty to the worlds."

Victory by permission — not by river discipline alone. Dawud (David), then a young figure in the army, kills Jalut; mulk and hikmah and taught knowledge follow later. Then a law of history: without Allah pushing people back by means of others, the earth would rot under unchecked tyranny. Daf' — checking, repelling — is a bounty, even when it arrives as struggle.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, said Allah may help this religion with a wicked man, and he taught that a just force restraining oppression is mercy for the earth. Pacifism that leaves the earth to predators is not the theology of this ayah; chaos without rules is not either.

Ask for permission-based victory. Accept that pushing back corruption may require human means He chooses. Bounty sometimes wears the face of a hard day on which a Dawud steps forward.

252:
"These are the verses of Allah which We recite to you in truth. And indeed, you are among the messengers."

A direct address to Muhammad, peace be upon him: these stories are Allah's ayat recited in truth — not borrowed myth, not evening entertainment. And you are of the mursalin. The seal on the Talut narrative is authentication of the narrator. He did not witness Dawud's battle with his eyes; revelation placed it on his tongue in truth.

The Prophet's messengerhood is the hinge of the surah. Denying him while enjoying the moral of his stories is unstable ground. Truth of recitation and truth of office rise together. He said he was given jawami' al-kalim — comprehensive speech — and that he does not speak from desire (53:3-4). This ayah is of that fabric.

Receive the stories as ayat, not as decoration only. The one to whom they were first recited was among the messengers — with all the obedience that office still demands from whoever says la ilaha illa Allah Muhammadun rasul Allah. If the story moved you, the messenger who brought it has a claim on your following, not only on your admiration.

253:
"Those messengers — some of them We caused to exceed others. Among them were those to whom Allah spoke, and He raised some of them in degree. And We gave Isa, the son of Maryam, clear proofs, and We supported him with the Pure Spirit. If Allah had willed, those succeeding them would not have fought each other after the clear proofs had come to them. But they differed, and some of them believed and some of them disbelieved. And if Allah had willed, they would not have fought each other, but Allah does what He intends."

Messengers are not identical in rank: Allah spoke to some (Musa), raised some in degrees (and Muhammad is the highest in the sunnah's witness), gave Isa bayyinat and support of the Ruh al-Qudus, Jibril. Preference is Allah's to assign; rivalry between their followers is not thereby justified. Fighting after clear proofs came is blamed on human difference — some believe, some disbelieve — within a will of Allah that allows history's test without loving the crime.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, forbade us to prefer him in a way that diminishes other prophets in disrespect, and he said do not make distinctions in the sense of rejecting some (2:285). Degrees exist; contempt does not follow.

Honour all messengers, know that ranks differ, and do not baptise sectarian wars as loyalty to a prophet who would not have joined your feud.

Ethics in conflict are part of faith, not decoration after victory. The same Book that allows force fences it. If your anger cannot accept a fence, it is not yet fighting in the way of Allah.
254:
"O you who believe, spend from that which We have provided for you before there comes a Day in which there is no exchange and no friendship and no intercession. And the disbelievers — they are the wrongdoers."

Spend from what We gave you — so the money is a trust returning through charity — before a Day with no bay' (no buying out of trouble), no khullah (no special friendship of the worldly kind that can pull strings), and no shafa'ah without His permission as other verses detail. Disbelievers are named the wrongdoers: the ultimate zulm is meeting that Day having refused the Giver while clutching His gifts.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, said give charity before a time when you will search for someone to accept it and not find them, and he said the people of wealth will have little reward except those who spend this way and that — right and left, open and secret. He stood in prayer until his feet swelled and still spent as if he would never need a coin tomorrow.

Move wealth now while exchange still works. On that Day you will want a receipt from this one. Friendship will not cash. Intercession will not be a market. Start the transfer — even if small — before the market of dunya closes and the only currency left is what you already sent ahead.

255:
"Allah — there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of existence. Neither drowsiness overtakes Him nor sleep. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission? He knows what is before them and what will be after them, and they encompass not a thing of His knowledge except for what He wills. His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth, and their preservation tires Him not. And He is the Most High, the Most Great."

Ayat al-Kursi, the greatest ayah in the Quran as the Prophet, peace be upon him, told Abu bin Ka'b. It moves from pure tawhid to Life and Qayyum sustenance, to freedom from drowsiness and sleep, to cosmic ownership, to intercession only by permission, to knowledge that surrounds all while none surround His knowledge except by His will, to the Kursi that spans heaven and earth, to preservation that never tires Him, to 'Aliyy and 'Azim.

He taught reading it after each fard prayer and before sleep for protection. It is creed as fortress: the heart that holds it cannot long believe in independent charms, rival gods, or a universe on autopilot.

Memorise it. Recite it. Let each clause demolish a fear: sleep does not take Him, so you may sleep; intercession is by permission, so you ask Him first; preservation does not tire Him, so your world is not held by your anxiety. The Most High, the Most Great — bigger than the night you are afraid of.

256:
"There is no compulsion in religion. The right course has become clear from the wrong. So whoever disbelieves in taghut and believes in Allah has grasped the most trustworthy handhold, which will never break. And Allah is Hearing and Knowing."

No ikrah in din — faith cannot be forced into a chest. Clarity is already distinct from error; the human must choose. Whoever rejects taghut (false objects of worship and obedience that rival Allah) and believes in Allah has hold of al-'urwah al-wuthqa, the firmest handhold, unbreakable. Hearing and Knowing watch the sincerity of that grasp.

This does not erase lawful order, parental teaching, or the combat verses against persecution; it erases inquisitorial forced conversion of conscience. The Prophet, peace be upon him, did not crack open chests. He conveyed, and Allah guided whom He willed. He said the firmest handhold of faith is to love and hate for Allah, and he wrote to kings inviting without inventing a sword as the first paragraph.

Offer Islam with clarity, not coercion. For yourself, grab the handhold with both hands: kufr bi al-taghut and iman billah. It will not snap when markets snap, when friends leave, when fear arrives. Hearing and Knowing mean the grip you claim in public and the grip you actually have in private are both already seen.

257:
"Allah is the ally of those who believe. He brings them out of darknesses into the light. And those who disbelieve — their allies are taghut. They take them out of the light into darknesses. Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide eternally therein."

Wilayah split in two. Allah is wali of the believers, pulling them from darknesses — plural — into light — singular. False gods and leaders as taghut pull the other way: from light into darknesses. One destination of that second path is named without softening: Fire, forever.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, said Allah is the wali of those who believe, and he taught that a person is with whom he loves. Choose allies the way you choose light sources. Multiple darknesses include doubt, lust, oppression, superstition, despair; the light of guidance is one in its source even if it spreads on many paths of obedience. He also said beware of sitting with the dead — and explained them as those who forget Allah.

If your friendships, feeds, and heroes keep dragging you from prayer into confusion, you may have found taghut in modern dress. Switch wilayah. The exit from darknesses is Allah as wali — not a mood, not a brand, not a crowd. The Fire at the end of the wrong wilayah is why this verse does not treat alliance as a light social preference.

258:
"Have you not considered the one who argued with Ibrahim about his Lord because Allah had given him kingship? When Ibrahim said, 'My Lord is the one who gives life and causes death,' he said, 'I give life and cause death.' Ibrahim said, 'Indeed, Allah brings up the sun from the east, so bring it up from the west.' So the disbeliever was confounded. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people."

A king (Namrud in the reports) argues because mulk inflated him. Ibrahim offers life and death as Allah's act; the king answers with cheap theatre — pardoning one prisoner and killing another. Ibrahim rises to a sign the king cannot stage: bring the sun from the west. The denier is confounded. Allah does not guide the zalim people — those who use power to bully truth rather than to seek it.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, admired Ibrahim as khalil and father of this ummah's millah. Argument for him was invitation with bayan, not sophistry. When a tyrant changes definitions of life and death, move the debate to what his hands cannot reach.

Do not let small power make you a Namrud in a meeting room. And when you face one, hold Ibrahim's calm clarity. Guidance is withheld from wrongdoing that has become identity.

259:
"Or like the one who passed by a township which had fallen upon its roofs. He said, 'How will Allah bring this to life after its death?' So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years; then He revived him. He said, 'How long have you remained?' The man said, 'I have remained a day or part of a day.' He said, 'Rather, you have remained one hundred years. Look at your food and your drink; it has not changed with time. And look at your donkey; and We will make you a sign for the people. And look at the bones — how We raise them and then We cover them with flesh.' And when it became clear to him, he said, 'I know that Allah is over all things competent.'"

A man (often identified in tafsir with Uzayr or another righteous figure) sees ruin and asks how revival is possible — not necessarily as denial, but as wonder that needs teaching. Allah makes him taste death for a hundred years and raises him. Food preserved, donkey decayed then reassembled in front of him: two signs in one lesson. He concludes with power over all things.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, affirmed bodily resurrection against Arab mockery, and the Quran repeatedly uses re-greening of land as the nearest analogy (22:5). This story is that analogy made personal and unforgettable.

When your mind staggers at graves, remember the hundred-year sleep and the fresh food. Competence is not strained by bones. He who started you first can start you again (36:79).

260:
"And when Ibrahim said, 'My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.' He said, 'Do you not believe?' He said, 'Yes, but that my heart may be satisfied.' He said, 'Take four birds and commit them to yourself. Then put on each hill a portion of them; then call them — they will come flying to you in haste. And know that Allah is Exalted in Might and Wise.'"

Ibrahim believes and still asks to see how. Allah's question "Have you not believed?" draws the beautiful answer: bala — yes — but that my heart be at ease. Faith has levels; seeing the how after accepting the what is a request for itminan, not a confession of kufr. The birds cut and scattered, then called back alive, teach gathering after dispersal by His might and wisdom.

The Prophet, peace be upon him, said that we have more right to doubt than Ibrahim — meaning Ibrahim's request was not shameful — and he praised the strong heart that seeks certainty. Aziz and Hakim close the demonstration: power to revive, wisdom in how the lesson is designed.

Ask for a satisfied heart through halal means: knowledge, reflection, righteous company, du'a. The father of this millah wanted ease of heart and was taught, not scolded off the path. Might and wisdom still answer those who already said bala and want their chest to catch up.
